---
title: "Comparing categories"
description: "Bars, lollipops, dumbbells, slopes, ranks, bridges and Likert scales."
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(ddplot)
library(ggplot2) # mpg, diamonds
library(dplyr)
```

Charts for comparing values across categories, from the everyday bar chart to before/after comparisons, rankings over time and bridges that explain how a total was built. Most of them expect data that is already aggregated, one row per category; `dplyr::summarise()` is a convenient way to get there.

::: {.dd-chooser}

| Chart | Use it when |
|---|---|
| [`bar_chart()`](#bar_chart) | You compare a value across categories, optionally split into grouped or stacked bars |
| [`horz_bar_chart()`](#horz_bar_chart) | You have many categories or long labels, or want 100% stacked bars |
| [`lollipop_chart()`](#lollipop_chart) | You want a lighter alternative to a bar chart, for many similar values |
| [`horz_lollipop()`](#horz_lollipop) | A lollipop chart with many categories or long labels |
| [`dumbbell_chart()`](#dumbbell_chart) | You show the gap between two values for each category |
| [`slope_chart()`](#slope_chart) | You compare two points in time and want to show who rose and who fell |
| [`bump_chart()`](#bump_chart) | You follow how rankings change over several periods |
| [`waterfall_chart()`](#waterfall_chart) | You explain how a starting value becomes a final value |
| [`radar_chart()`](#radar_chart) | You compare a few items across several variables |
| [`radial_bar_chart()`](#radial_bar_chart) | You show progress of a few items towards a goal |
| [`likert_chart()`](#likert_chart) | You show survey answers on an agree / disagree scale for several questions |

:::

## `bar_chart()` {#bar_chart}

`bar_chart()` draws one bar per category. Hover a bar to read its value, its share of the total and its rank. The buttons at the top right re-sort the bars (original order, largest first, smallest first) with an animation.

```{r}
library(dplyr)

mpg %>%
  group_by(manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(mean_cty = mean(cty)) %>%
  bar_chart(
    x = "manufacturer",
    y = "mean_cty",
    sort = "descending",
    highlight = c("honda", "volkswagen"),
    value_format = ".1f",
    y_title = "Average city miles per gallon",
    title = "City fuel economy by manufacturer",
    subtitle = "Honda and Volkswagen lead the field"
  )
```

`highlight` keeps some bars in colour and greys out the others.

### Counting and aggregating

You do not have to aggregate first. Leave `y` empty to count the rows of each category, or set `agg` to `"mean"`, `"median"`, `"min"` or `"max"` (the default, `"sum"`, adds the rows up):

```{r}
bar_chart(mpg, x = "class", sort = "descending", title = "Cars per class")
```

```{r}
bar_chart(mpg, x = "class", y = "hwy", agg = "median", sort = "descending",
          title = "Median highway miles per gallon by class")
```

### Groups: grouped, stacked and 100%

`group` splits each bar by a second variable. Use the **Grouped / Stacked / 100%** buttons to switch layouts; the legend hides a group on click and keeps only that group on double-click.

```{r}
bar_chart(
  data = mpg,
  x = "class",
  group = "drv",
  sort = "descending",
  fill = c("4" = "#4269d0", "f" = "#efb118", "r" = "#ff725c"),
  title = "Cars per class and drive train"
)
```

`position` sets the starting layout. Stacked bars show a total above each bar, and `ref_lines` draws a target or an average:

```{r}
sales <- data.frame(
  quarter = rep(c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"), each = 3),
  region  = rep(c("North", "South", "West"), 4),
  revenue = c(120, 95, 60, 135, 90, 72, 150, 110, 80, 170, 105, 96)
)

bar_chart(
  sales,
  x = "quarter",
  y = "revenue",
  group = "region",
  position = "stacked",
  ref_lines = c(Target = 300),
  value_prefix = "$",
  value_suffix = "k",
  title = "Revenue by quarter"
)
```

### In Shiny

Clicking a bar sets `input$<id>_clicked` to the clicked `category` and `group`. The chosen layout, sort order and hidden groups are kept when the chart is updated:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
output$classes <- renderD3(bar_chart(mpg, "class", group = "drv"))
observeEvent(input$classes_clicked, {
  print(input$classes_clicked$category)
})
```

## `horz_bar_chart()` {#horz_bar_chart}

`horz_bar_chart()` is the horizontal version, better for many categories or long labels. It has the same features; only the names of the first arguments differ (`label` for the categories, `value` for the numbers).

```{r}
mpg %>%
  group_by(manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(median_hwy = median(hwy)) %>%
  horz_bar_chart(
    label = "manufacturer",
    value = "median_hwy",
    sort = "descending",
    value_title = "Median highway miles per gallon",
    title = "Highway fuel economy by manufacturer"
  )
```

A 100% stacked layout shows the composition of each category:

```{r}
horz_bar_chart(
  data = mpg,
  label = "manufacturer",
  group = "drv",
  position = "percent",
  sort = "descending",
  title = "Drive train by manufacturer"
)
```

Negative values grow to the left of zero; `negative_fill` gives them their own colour:

```{r}
growth <- data.frame(
  country = c("Spain", "France", "Italy", "Germany", "Poland", "Sweden"),
  gdp     = c(2.4, 0.9, -0.3, -0.6, 3.1, 1.2)
)

horz_bar_chart(
  growth,
  label = "country",
  value = "gdp",
  sort = "descending",
  negative_fill = "#ff725c",
  value_suffix = "%",
  value_title = "GDP growth",
  title = "Annual GDP growth (illustrative data)"
)
```

## `lollipop_chart()` {#lollipop_chart}

`lollipop_chart()` is a lighter alternative to a bar chart: each value is a thin stem ending in a dot, which keeps the chart readable when many categories have similar values. It works like `bar_chart()`: hover a lollipop to read its value and its rank, and use the buttons at the top right to re-sort the lollipops.

```{r}
mpg %>%
  group_by(manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(mean_hwy = mean(hwy)) %>%
  lollipop_chart(
    x = "manufacturer",
    y = "mean_hwy",
    sort = "descending",
    y_title = "Average highway miles per gallon",
    title = "Highway fuel economy by manufacturer",
    highlight = c("honda", "toyota"),
    value_format = ".1f"
  )
```

You can pass raw rows: they are combined with `agg` (`"sum"` by default, or `"mean"`, `"median"`, `"min"`, `"max"`, `"count"`), and leaving `y` empty counts the rows. With `group`, each category gets one lollipop per group; click a legend entry to hide a group, double-click it to keep only that group.

```{r}
lollipop_chart(
  mpg,
  x = "class",
  y = "cty",
  group = "year",
  agg = "mean",
  sort = "descending",
  value_format = ".1f",
  title = "City miles per gallon, 1999 and 2008"
)
```

The look is set with `circle_fill`, `circle_radius`, `line_stroke` and `line_stroke_width`. Values below zero are drawn downwards, in `negative_fill` if you give one:

```{r}
change <- data.frame(
  country = c("Spain", "France", "Italy", "Germany", "Poland", "Sweden"),
  growth  = c(2.4, 0.9, -0.3, -0.6, 3.1, 1.2)
)

lollipop_chart(
  change,
  x = "country",
  y = "growth",
  negative_fill = "#ff725c",
  value_suffix = "%",
  y_title = "GDP growth",
  title = "Annual GDP growth",
  circle_radius = 8,
  line_stroke = "#c9ced6"
)
```

In Shiny, clicking a lollipop sets `input$<id>_clicked` to its `category` and `group`, and the sort order and hidden groups are kept when the chart is re-rendered.

## `horz_lollipop()` {#horz_lollipop}

`horz_lollipop()` is the horizontal version, for many categories or long labels. It takes the same arguments, with `label` and `value` instead of `x` and `y`.

```{r}
mpg %>%
  group_by(manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(median_cty = median(cty)) %>%
  horz_lollipop(
    label = "manufacturer",
    value = "median_cty",
    sort = "descending",
    value_title = "Median city miles per gallon",
    title = "City fuel economy by manufacturer"
  )
```

Counting rows, with the average as a reference line:

```{r}
counts <- count(mpg, manufacturer)

horz_lollipop(
  mpg,
  label = "manufacturer",
  sort = "descending",
  ref_lines = c(Average = mean(counts$n)),
  value_title = "Number of models",
  title = "Models per manufacturer"
)
```

## `dumbbell_chart()` {#dumbbell_chart}

A dumbbell chart (also called a connected dot plot) shows two values per category as dots joined by a horizontal line. It is the clearest way to communicate the gap or change between two groups, time points, or conditions across many categories , a grouped bar chart would require much more visual scanning to reach the same conclusion. The New York Times and The Economist use this format regularly.

```{r}
life_exp <- data.frame(
  country   = c("Brazil", "China", "Egypt", "India",
                "Japan", "Mexico", "Nigeria", "Turkey"),
  year_1952 = c(50.9, 44.0, 41.9, 37.4, 63.0, 50.8, 36.3, 43.6),
  year_2007 = c(72.4, 72.9, 71.3, 64.7, 82.6, 76.2, 46.9, 71.8)
)

dumbbell_chart(
  data     = life_exp,
  x1       = "year_1952",
  x2       = "year_2007",
  y        = "country",
  x1_label  = "1952",
  x2_label  = "2007",
  title    = "Life expectancy: 1952 vs 2007",
  x_title   = "Life expectancy (years)",
  sort     = "ascending"
)
```

The chart works equally well for comparing two conditions within the same time period. Here we compare average city and highway fuel economy across vehicle classes using the `mpg` dataset:

```{r}
library(dplyr)

mpg_summary <- mpg |>
  group_by(class) |>
  summarise(city = mean(cty), highway = mean(hwy))

dumbbell_chart(
  data    = mpg_summary,
  x1      = "city",
  x2      = "highway",
  y       = "class",
  x1_label = "City",
  x2_label = "Highway",
  col1    = "steelblue",
  col2    = "darkorange",
  title   = "City vs highway fuel economy by class",
  x_title  = "Miles per gallon",
  sort    = "ascending"
)
```

## `slope_chart()` {#slope_chart}

A slope chart (or slopegraph) places two values per category on two vertical axes, typically "before" and "after" or two different years, and connects them with a straight line. The steepness and direction of each line tell you at a glance who rose, who fell, and how the ranking changed. Edward Tufte popularised the form in *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information* (1983) with his chart of government receipts across rich countries, and the New York Times graphics desk has used it regularly ever since. Use it when you have a small-to-moderate number of categories measured at exactly two points; with many categories or many time points, a line chart is the better choice.

Each line is labelled with its category name and value at both ends, and labels that would overlap are nudged apart vertically. By default lines are colored by direction (increase or decrease). Hover over a line to emphasise it and fade the others.

```{r}
# Current receipts of government as a percentage of GDP, 1970 vs 1979
# (adapted from Edward Tufte's classic slopegraph)
receipts <- data.frame(
  country = c("Sweden", "Netherlands", "Norway", "Britain", "France",
              "Germany", "Belgium", "Canada", "Finland", "Italy",
              "United States", "Greece", "Switzerland", "Spain", "Japan"),
  y1970 = c(46.9, 44.0, 43.5, 40.7, 39.0, 37.5, 35.2, 35.2, 34.9, 30.4,
            30.3, 26.8, 26.5, 22.5, 20.7),
  y1979 = c(57.4, 55.8, 52.2, 39.0, 43.4, 42.9, 43.2, 35.8, 38.2, 35.7,
            32.5, 30.6, 33.2, 27.1, 26.6)
)

slope_chart(
  data       = receipts,
  start      = "y1970",
  end        = "y1979",
  group      = "country",
  start_label = "1970",
  end_label   = "1979",
  digits     = 1,
  title      = "Government receipts as % of GDP",
  height     = 520
)
```

Use `highlight` to tell a story about a few categories: the rest are drawn in a muted grey so they give context without competing for attention. Here we compare life expectancy in 1952 and 2007 using the `gapminder` dataset:

```{r}
library(gapminder)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

countries <- c("China", "India", "Japan", "Brazil", "Nigeria",
               "Egypt", "Germany", "United States", "South Africa")

life <- filter(gapminder, year %in% c(1952, 2007), country %in% countries)
life <- select(life, country, year, lifeExp)
life <- pivot_wider(life, names_from = year, values_from = lifeExp,
                    names_prefix = "y")

slope_chart(
  data       = life,
  start      = "y1952",
  end        = "y2007",
  group      = "country",
  start_label = "1952",
  end_label   = "2007",
  highlight  = c("China", "South Africa"),
  digits     = 1,
  title      = "Life expectancy: 1952 vs 2007"
)
```

## `bump_chart()` {#bump_chart}

A bump chart shows how the *rank* of several entities changes from one period to the next. Each entity is a smooth line that climbs or falls as it overtakes, or is overtaken by, the others, and a circle at every period displays its rank. The Financial Times, The Economist and FiveThirtyEight use this format for league tables, polls and country rankings: it is the right choice when the order matters more than the exact values.

The data must be in long format, with one row per entity and period. By default `bump_chart()` computes the ranks for each period from the numeric `y` column (rank 1 = highest value, use `rank_order = "asc"` to reverse). If your `y` column already holds ranks, set `ranked = TRUE`. Hover over a line to make it stand out.

```{r}
league <- data.frame(
  season = rep(c("2023", "2024", "2025", "2026"), each = 5),
  team   = rep(c("Lions", "Tigers", "Bears", "Wolves", "Eagles"), 4),
  points = c(80, 75, 60, 55, 50,
             70, 82, 58, 66, 49,
             65, 78, 72, 69, 52,
             60, 74, 81, 70, 77)
)

bump_chart(
  data  = league,
  x     = "season",
  y     = "points",
  group = "team",
  title = "League ranking by season"
)
```

Use `highlight` to bring a few entities forward and grey out the rest. Here are the GDP per capita ranks of eight Asian economies from the `gapminder` dataset:

```{r}
library(gapminder)

countries <- c("Japan", "Singapore", "Hong Kong, China", "Taiwan",
               "Korea, Rep.", "Malaysia", "Thailand", "China")

gdp <- gapminder[gapminder$country %in% countries & gapminder$year >= 1967, ]
gdp$country <- as.character(gdp$country)

bump_chart(
  data      = gdp,
  x         = "year",
  y         = "gdpPercap",
  group     = "country",
  highlight = c("Singapore", "Korea, Rep."),
  title     = "GDP per capita rank, 1967-2007"
)
```

## `waterfall_chart()` {#waterfall_chart}

A waterfall chart shows how an initial value is built up or eroded by a sequence of positive and negative contributions. Each bar starts exactly where the previous one ended. It is the standard chart for P&L decomposition, budget variance analysis, and any "what changed and why" narrative.

The optional `measure` column lets you mark certain bars as `"total"`, they span from zero to the running cumulative sum, making subtotals and final totals visually distinct. **Hovering over any bar shows a tooltip** with the label, the delta, and the running total.

```{r}
pnl <- data.frame(
  label   = c("Revenue", "COGS", "Gross Profit",
              "R&D", "S&M", "G&A", "Operating Income"),
  value   = c(1200, -450, 750, -120, -90, -60, 480),
  measure = c("relative", "relative", "total",
              "relative", "relative", "relative", "total")
)

waterfall_chart(
  data   = pnl,
  x      = "label",
  y      = "value",
  measure = "measure",
  title  = "P&L bridge",
  y_title = "USD thousands"
)
```

Without a `measure` column every bar is a simple delta — useful for tracking a running balance over time:

```{r}
cashflow <- data.frame(
  month = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun"),
  delta = c(120, -30, 80, -60, 95, -20)
)

waterfall_chart(
  data          = cashflow,
  x             = "month",
  y             = "delta",
  title         = "Monthly cash flow",
  y_title        = "USD thousands",
  positive_color = "steelblue",
  negative_color = "tomato"
)
```

## `radar_chart()` {#radar_chart}

`radar_chart()` draws one translucent polygon per series over a polygonal grid, with one spoke per variable. Its look and feel is inspired by the radar chart of [Chart.js](https://www.chartjs.org/). Polygons grow out from the center, hovering over a point shows its value, and clicking a legend entry toggles that series.

```{r}
players <- data.frame(
  player    = c("Ana", "Ben", "Chloe"),
  speed     = c(88, 72, 65),
  power     = c(60, 91, 70),
  passing   = c(79, 58, 93),
  dribbling = c(92, 64, 81),
  defending = c(45, 83, 74),
  stamina   = c(70, 77, 88)
)

radar_chart(
  data     = players,
  group    = "player",
  axes     = c("speed", "power", "passing", "dribbling", "defending", "stamina"),
  max_value = 100,
  title    = "Player skill ratings"
)
```

When the variables are measured in different units, `scale_each_axis = TRUE` gives each axis its own scale:

```{r}
cyl_means <- aggregate(cbind(mpg, hp, wt, qsec, disp) ~ cyl, data = mtcars, FUN = mean)
cyl_means$cyl <- paste(cyl_means$cyl, "cylinders")

radar_chart(
  data          = cyl_means,
  group         = "cyl",
  axis_labels    = c("Miles/gallon", "Horsepower", "Weight (1000 lbs)",
                    "1/4 mile time (s)", "Displacement (cu.in.)"),
  scale_each_axis = TRUE,
  levels        = 4,
  grid_shape     = "circle",
  value_format   = ".1f",
  title         = "mtcars averages by number of cylinders"
)
```

## `radial_bar_chart()` {#radial_bar_chart}

`radial_bar_chart()` draws each category as a concentric circular progress track, inspired by the radialBar chart of [ApexCharts](https://apexcharts.com/). Each ring has a faint background track and a rounded arc that sweeps in on load, a label sits at the start of each track, and the average (or total) is shown in the center. Hover over a ring to put its name and value in the center.

```{r}
platforms <- data.frame(
  platform = c("Vimeo", "Messenger", "Facebook", "LinkedIn"),
  share    = c(76, 67, 61, 90)
)

radial_bar_chart(
  data  = platforms,
  label = "platform",
  value = "share",
  title = "Weekly active users (share of total, illustrative)"
)
```

With `max` you can set the value that fills a whole ring, and with `end_angle = 360` the tracks make a full circle:

```{r}
sales <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "East", "West", "Central"),
  units  = c(420, 310, 275, 190, 120)
)

radial_bar_chart(
  data        = sales,
  label       = "region",
  value       = "units",
  max         = 500,
  end_angle    = 360,
  center_value = "total",
  center_label = "Units sold",
  title       = "Units sold by region (target: 500)"
)
```

## `likert_chart()` {#likert_chart}

A Likert chart shows answers on an ordered scale as diverging bars: the negative answers go left of the centre line, the positive ones right, and a neutral answer (the middle of an odd scale) sits across the line. The totals of negative and positive answers are written at both ends. Give one row per answer, or counts in a `value` column; `levels` sets the order of the scale. Hover an answer to highlight it for every question.

```{r}
survey <- data.frame(
  question = rep(c("The product is easy to use", "Support answers quickly",
                   "The price is fair", "I would recommend it"), each = 5),
  answer = rep(c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree",
                 "Strongly agree"), times = 4),
  n = c(4, 10, 18, 45, 23,  12, 20, 25, 28, 15,  20, 30, 22, 20, 8,
        5, 8, 15, 40, 32)
)
likert_chart(survey, question = "question", response = "answer", value = "n",
             sort = "positive", title = "Customer survey")
```

A scale with an even number of levels has no neutral answer:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
scale4 <- c("Never", "Rarely", "Often", "Always")
habits <- data.frame(
  habit = rep(c("Cook at home", "Walk to work", "Read before bed"), each = 60),
  answer = c(sample(scale4, 60, TRUE, c(1, 2, 4, 3)),
             sample(scale4, 60, TRUE, c(4, 3, 2, 1)),
             sample(scale4, 60, TRUE, c(2, 3, 3, 2)))
)
likert_chart(habits, question = "habit", response = "answer", levels = scale4,
             colors = c("#d6402b", "#ffb15c", "#6cc5b0", "#1f7a63"))
```
